title: Dockerfile Essentials
intro: You've built images from an existing Dockerfile — now let's look at the instructions themselves and a couple of build-time debugging tricks.

steps.prompt: Build an image using a specific Dockerfile named 'Dockerfile.prod' instead of the default 'Dockerfile'.
steps.fake_output:
Step 1/6 : FROM node:20-alpine AS build
Step 2/6 : FROM node:20-alpine
...
Successfully built abc123
Successfully tagged myapp:prod
steps.explanation: -f points at a specific Dockerfile — common when you keep separate dev/prod Dockerfiles, or a multi-stage build split across files.
steps.why: Without -f, docker build always looks for a file literally named 'Dockerfile' in the build context — -f is required the moment you deviate from that default name.

steps.prompt: Notice the output showed two FROM lines — this is a multi-stage build. Check the image size to confirm the final image doesn't include the build stage's tools.
steps.fake_output:
REPOSITORY   TAG    IMAGE ID   SIZE
myapp        prod   abc123     52MB
steps.explanation: 52MB is small because only the FINAL stage (FROM node:20-alpine, no build tools) ends up in the shipped image — the first stage's compilers/build dependencies are discarded.
steps.why: This is the entire point of multi-stage builds: 'FROM node:20-alpine AS build' does the npm install/compile work in a throwaway stage, then a later 'COPY --from=build' pulls only the compiled output into a clean final stage — you get small production images without needing a separate cleanup step.

steps.prompt: Build without using any cached layers, to rule out a stale cache as the cause of a weird bug.
steps.fake_output:
Step 1/5 : FROM node:20-alpine
 ---> Pulling fresh
Step 3/5 : RUN npm install
 ---> Running (no cache)
Successfully built d4e5f6
steps.explanation: Every layer rebuilds from scratch — slower, but rules out 'the cache is lying to me' as a variable when debugging a build that behaves unexpectedly.
steps.why: This is specifically the fix that resolves docker-incident-001 (Container Keeps Exiting Immediately) if the actual root cause was a stale cached layer from before a Dockerfile fix — a normal 'docker build' can keep reusing a broken cached layer even after you've fixed the instruction that created it.

steps.prompt: Pass a build-time argument for the app version into the build.
steps.fake_output:
Step 2/5 : ARG VERSION=1.0.0
Step 3/5 : RUN echo "Building version $VERSION"
 ---> Building version 2.1.0
Successfully built e5f6g7
steps.explanation: ARG values only exist during the build itself — unlike ENV, they are NOT available inside the running container unless you explicitly copy the value into an ENV instruction too.
steps.why: This ARG-vs-ENV distinction is the single most common Dockerfile confusion: ARG is a build-time-only input (like a version string baked into the build), ENV is a runtime variable the running container can actually read — mixing them up is exactly what causes 'why is my env var empty inside the container' bugs.

steps.prompt: Confirm the running container's health check is passing.
steps.explanation: This reads the result of the Dockerfile's HEALTHCHECK instruction — Docker runs that check on an interval and tracks healthy/unhealthy/starting status automatically.
steps.why: Without a HEALTHCHECK, 'docker ps' only ever shows 'Up' for a running container, even if the app inside has deadlocked and stopped actually serving requests — HEALTHCHECK is what lets Docker (and orchestrators built on top of it) tell the difference between a process that's alive and an app that's actually working.
